concept.technique_name: counting trailing zeros by successive division (Legendre's formula for the power of 5)

examples.problem_statement: If X is a natural number and X! ends with Y zeros then number of zeros at the end of (5X)! is

solution.description: Write the count of trailing zeros of X! as the sum of the successive quotients of X by 5, 25, 125, ...; the book names this whole sum Y.
Apply the same successive-division sum to (5X)!, dividing 5X in turn by 5, 25, 125, and so on.
Simplify each term of the (5X)! sum: it becomes X followed by exactly the sum written in step 1, so the total is X plus Y.
Check the relationship by trial with concrete values, as the book does: for X = 10 and for X = 20 the zero count of (5X)! equals X + Y in both cases.

key_reminders: Trailing zeros of a factorial are counted by the successive quotients [N/5] + [N/25] + [N/125] + ... , keeping only the integer part of each division.
Dividing 5X by 5, 25, 125, ... reproduces the term list for X shifted by one place, with the leading term equal to X itself.
The book verifies the general result by substituting concrete natural numbers for X.
common_mistakes: Stopping the successive-division sum at [N/5] and missing the higher powers 25, 125, ... that also contribute zeros.
Assuming the zero count scales by a factor of 5 (giving 5Y) instead of shifting the term list to give X + Y.

concept.technique_name: work equation W = RT applied twice to a shared job size

examples.problem_statement: Machine A, which produces 15 golf clubs per hour, fills a production lot in 6 hours. Machine B fills the same production lot in 1.5 hours. How many golf clubs does Machine B produce per hour?

solution.operation: W = RT = (15 \text{ clubs per hour})(6 \text{ hours})
solution.description: Put Machine A's rate and time into the work formula W = RT to find how much work one production lot represents.
Carry the lot size of 90 clubs over to Machine B, which fills the same lot, and rewrite its 1.5 hours as 3/2 to make the division easier, as the book directs.
Use W = RT a second time for Machine B, dividing its work by its time to get its hourly rate.

key_reminders: W = RT: with any two of work, rate and time known, the third follows.
Both machines fill the same production lot, so the work value found from Machine A is reused for Machine B.
Converting 1.5 hours to 3/2 turns the division into a multiplication by 2/3's reciprocal and keeps the arithmetic exact.
common_mistakes: Dividing by 1.5 as though it were a rate rather than a time, or multiplying 90 by 1.5 instead of dividing.
Reporting the lot size 90 as the answer instead of continuing to Machine B's per-hour rate.

concept.technique_name: mean of a frequency distribution (weighted sum divided by total frequency)

examples.problem_statement: The table above shows the frequency distribution of the values of a variable Y. What is the mean of the distribution? Give your answer to the nearest 0.01.

solution.description: Rather than writing each repeated value out one at a time, multiply every value of Y by the frequency next to it in the table and add the products; the book's total is 44.
Add down the Frequency column to get how many values of Y there are in all.
Divide the summed values by the number of values, which is what the mean of the distribution means.
Round the decimal quotient to two decimal places, as the question's instruction requires.

key_reminders: The mean of a distribution is the sum of all values divided by the number of values.
In a frequency table, a value repeated f times contributes value times f to the sum, and f to the count.
The number of values is the sum of the Frequency column, not the number of table rows.
common_mistakes: Dividing 44 by the number of distinct rows (5) instead of by the total frequency 34.
Truncating 1.2941... to 1.294 or 1.30 instead of rounding to the required nearest 0.01.
